question: 'Long Walk to Freedom' is an autobiography of ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nelson Mandela.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• 'Long Walk to Freedom' (1994) is the autobiography of Nelson Mandela, the anti-apartheid leader who became the first black President of South Africa (1994–1999). (आत्मकथा — autobiography)

• Much of the book was drafted secretly while Mandela was imprisoned on Robben Island; he spent 27 years in jail.

• Mandela received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 (jointly with F. W. de Klerk) and India's Bharat Ratna in 1990 — the second foreigner after Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Mahatma Gandhi — 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth' (originally in Gujarati, 'Satya Na Prayogo').

• Benjamin Franklin — 'The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin'; he was a founding father of the USA.

• Jawaharlal Nehru — 'An Autobiography' (also 'Toward Freedom'), plus 'The Discovery of India' and 'Glimpses of World History'.

NOTE

• Other famous autobiographies: 'Wings of Fire' — A. P. J. Abdul Kalam; 'My Truth' — Indira Gandhi; 'Playing It My Way' — Sachin Tendulkar; 'Unbreakable' — Mary Kom.

• Nelson Mandela International Day is observed on 18 July, his birthday.

question: The Himalayan mountain range is a type of ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is fold mountains.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Himalayas are fold mountains (वलित पर्वत), formed by the compression and folding of sediments of the Tethys Sea when the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate.

• They are the youngest fold mountains in the world and are still rising, which makes the region seismically active.

• The three parallel ranges from north to south are the Himadri (Greater Himalayas), Himachal (Lesser Himalayas) and Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Residual (relict) mountains are formed by prolonged erosion of older highlands — e.g., the Aravallis, Nilgiris, Parasnath.

• Block mountains are formed when land between faults is uplifted or the surrounding land subsides — e.g., the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, the Black Forest of Germany.

• Accumulated mountains are heaps of sand, gravel or volcanic material, not a classification the Himalayas belong to.

NOTE

• Other major fold mountains: Alps (Europe), Andes (South America), Rockies (North America), Atlas (Africa).

• Mount Everest (8,848.86 m) in Nepal is the highest Himalayan peak; Kangchenjunga is the highest peak located in India (Sikkim).

question: Negative ions that consist of a single atom are named by adding the suffix ______ to the stem of the name of the element.
solution_text:
The correct answer is -ide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A monatomic anion (single-atom negative ion) is named by taking the stem of the element's name and adding the suffix -ide. (ऋणायन — anion)

• Examples: Cl⁻ → chloride, O²⁻ → oxide, N³⁻ → nitride, S²⁻ → sulphide, H⁻ → hydride.

• Hence ionic compounds are named as metal + non-metal-ide: NaCl — sodium chloride, CaO — calcium oxide, MgS — magnesium sulphide.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• -onium is used for certain positively charged (cationic) species, e.g., ammonium (NH₄⁺), hydronium (H₃O⁺).

• -ic and -ous are used in the older (classical) system to show the higher and lower oxidation state of a metal, e.g., ferric (Fe³⁺) and ferrous (Fe²⁺), cupric (Cu²⁺) and cuprous (Cu⁺).

NOTE

• Oxygen-containing polyatomic anions take -ate (more oxygen) and -ite (less oxygen): sulphate SO₄²⁻ / sulphite SO₃²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻ / nitrite NO₂⁻.

• A cation is positively charged (moves to the cathode); an anion is negatively charged (moves to the anode).

question: Major Dhyan Chand was famous for which sport?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Field hockey.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Major Dhyan Chand (1905–1979) was a legendary Indian field hockey player, known as 'The Wizard' / 'The Magician' of hockey for his extraordinary ball control. (हॉकी के जादूगर)

• He won three Olympic gold medals for India in hockey — Amsterdam 1928, Los Angeles 1932 and Berlin 1936 (he captained the 1936 team).

• National Sports Day is celebrated on 29 August, his birth anniversary, on which the Khel Ratna, Arjuna and Dronacharya awards are conferred.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• In August 2021 the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award was renamed the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award — India's highest sporting honour.

• Dhyan Chand received the Padma Bhushan in 1956.

• His brother Roop Singh and son Ashok Kumar were also Indian hockey internationals; Ashok Kumar scored in the 1975 World Cup final win.

NOTE

• Hockey is played 11-a-side; India won the Hockey World Cup in 1975 (Kuala Lumpur) and the bronze medal at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics (played 2021).

• The Dhyan Chand Award is given for lifetime achievement in sports.

question: Which article of the Indian constitution enshrines the right against exploitation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 23 and 24.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Right against Exploitation (शोषण के विरुद्ध अधिकार) is guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, in Part III (Fundamental Rights).

• Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour.

• Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below 14 years in any factory, mine or other hazardous employment.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Articles 25–28 deal with the Right to Freedom of Religion; Article 27 bars taxes for promotion of a religion and Article 28 restricts religious instruction in State-funded institutions.

• Article 21 guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty; Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) provides free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.

• Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

NOTE

• Six Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality (14–18), Right to Freedom (19–22), Right against Exploitation (23–24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25–28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29–30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (32).

• Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

question: Cytology is the study of _______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cells.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cytology (also called cell biology) is the branch of biology that deals with the structure, function and life processes of cells. (कोशिका विज्ञान)

• The cell is the structural and functional unit of life; it was discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665 in a thin slice of cork.

• Anton van Leeuwenhoek first observed living cells, and Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Genetics — the study of genes, heredity and variation; the term was coined by William Bateson, and Gregor Mendel is called the Father of Genetics.

• Histology — the study of tissues.

• Chloroplasts are studied within plant cell biology; they contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis.

NOTE

• Related branches: Osteology — bones; Nephrology — kidneys; Cardiology — heart; Ornithology — birds; Entomology — insects; Mycology — fungi.

• Cell Theory was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann (1838–39) and extended by Rudolf Virchow (1855) — 'Omnis cellula e cellula'.

question: The Amaravati School of art was developed under the patronage of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satavahanas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Amaravati School of Art flourished on the banks of the Krishna river in Andhra Pradesh under the patronage of the Satavahanas (roughly 2nd century BCE – 3rd century CE).

• It used white marble-like limestone, showed strong Buddhist themes (Jataka stories, the Mahachaitya/Great Stupa of Amaravati) and is noted for narrative panels full of movement and emotion. (अमरावती कला शैली)

• Unlike the Gandhara school, Amaravati art was indigenous in style with no Greek influence.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Cholas — famed for bronze sculpture (the Nataraja) and Dravidian temples like the Brihadeeswarar Temple, Thanjavur (Rajaraja I).

• Cheras — an ancient Sangam-age kingdom of the Kerala region.

• Palas of Bengal and Bihar patronised the Pala School of Buddhist art and the universities of Nalanda and Vikramshila.

NOTE

• Three great schools of ancient Indian art: Gandhara (Greco-Roman influence, grey sandstone, Kushana patronage), Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone, Kushana patronage), Amaravati (white limestone, Satavahana patronage).

• Simuka founded the Satavahana dynasty; Gautamiputra Satakarni was its greatest ruler.

question: The founder of Brahmo Sabha was ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 in Calcutta; it was later renamed the Brahmo Samaj. (ब्रह्म समाज)

• He is called the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance' and the 'Maker of Modern India'; he campaigned successfully for the abolition of Sati in 1829 under Lord William Bentinck.

• He opposed idol worship, caste rigidity and child marriage, and supported women's rights, widow remarriage and modern English education.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Rabindranath Tagore — Nobel laureate (1913, Gitanjali); his father Debendranath Tagore led the Brahmo Samaj after Roy and founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha.

• Radhakanta Deb founded the Dharma Sabha (1830), an orthodox body that opposed the abolition of Sati.

• Keshab Chandra Sen later split from the Samaj and formed the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866); his followers' work led to the Native Marriage Act, 1872.

NOTE

• Other reform bodies: Arya Samaj (1875) — Dayanand Saraswati; Prarthana Samaj (1867) — Atmaram Pandurang; Ramakrishna Mission (1897) — Swami Vivekananda; Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) — Jyotiba Phule.

• Roy published the newspapers Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) and Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian); the title 'Raja' was given by Mughal emperor Akbar II.

question: Which among the following soils is also known as Regur soil?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Black.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Black soil is also called Regur soil or 'black cotton soil' because it is ideally suited for growing cotton. (रेगुर मृदा)

• It is formed from the weathering of the Deccan lava (basalt) and is found mainly in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

• It is rich in iron, lime, calcium, magnesium, potash and aluminium but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter; it is highly moisture-retentive and develops deep cracks in summer, which self-ploughs the soil.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Alluvial soil — the most widespread and most fertile soil of India, deposited by rivers in the northern plains; rich in potash and lime, poor in nitrogen.

• Laterite soil — formed by intense leaching in areas of high temperature and heavy rainfall; suitable for tea, coffee, cashew.

• Peaty soil — found in areas of heavy rainfall and high humidity (Kerala's Kuttanad, coastal Odisha, Sundarbans); rich in humus and organic matter.

NOTE

• Black soil is the second most widespread soil in India after alluvial soil.

• Soil classification in India is done by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR); other types include red and yellow, arid/desert, saline and forest/mountain soils.

question: ______ refers to a method adopted by the Central Bank to persuade or convince the commercial banks to advance credit in the economic interest of the country.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Moral Suasion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Moral suasion is a qualitative (selective) instrument of monetary policy in which the central bank (RBI) persuades, advises or requests commercial banks to follow a desired credit policy — through letters, speeches and meetings. (नैतिक दबाव)

• It is persuasive, not statutory — there is no legal compulsion or penalty attached, so it is also called 'jawboning'.

• It is used, for example, to ask banks to restrict lending to speculative sectors or to expand credit to priority sectors.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) — a window (introduced in 2011) through which scheduled commercial banks borrow overnight funds from the RBI against approved securities; the MSF rate is above the repo rate.

• Credit rationing — the RBI fixes ceilings on the amount of credit for particular sectors or banks.

• Margin requirement — the difference between the value of the security offered and the loan granted; raising the margin reduces borrowing.

NOTE

• Quantitative tools: Bank Rate, Repo Rate, Reverse Repo, CRR, SLR, Open Market Operations. Qualitative tools: margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing, direct action, consumer credit regulation.

• The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 and nationalised on 1 January 1949; monetary policy is decided by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

question: In February 2022, Cabinet approved implementation of Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. Which ministry of central government launched the Ayushman Bharat Yojana across the country?
option_3: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
option_4: Ministry of Women and Child Development
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ayushman Bharat and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) are implemented by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW). (स्वास्थ्य एवं परिवार कल्याण मंत्रालय)

• Ayushman Bharat – PM Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) was launched on 23 September 2018 from Ranchi, Jharkhand, and provides health cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care; it is the world's largest health assurance scheme.

• The Cabinet approved the nationwide roll-out of ABDM in February 2022 with an outlay of ₹1,600 crore; it creates a digital health ecosystem with the ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) ID.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• National Health Authority (NHA) is the apex body implementing PM-JAY and ABDM.

• The second component of Ayushman Bharat is the network of Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs).

• The Ministry of Ayush handles Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy; it became a separate ministry in 2014.

NOTE

• Other MoHFW programmes: National Health Mission (NHM), Mission Indradhanush, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (Dept. of Pharmaceuticals).

• ABDM was first launched as the National Digital Health Mission on 15 August 2020 in six UTs on a pilot basis.

question: Who is the supreme commander of the defence forces of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is President of India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under Article 53(2) of the Constitution, the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union is vested in the President of India. (सर्वोच्च सेनापति)

• The President appoints the Chiefs of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and declarations of war and peace are made in the President's name — but always on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74).

• The President also confers gallantry awards such as the Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The Chief of Army Staff heads only the Indian Army; the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) — a post created in 2019, first held by General Bipin Rawat — is the single-point military adviser to the government.

• The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet Committee on Security, but is not the supreme commander.

• The Chief Justice of India heads the judiciary and administers the oath of office to the President.

NOTE

• Qualifications for President: citizen of India, 35 years of age, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha (Article 58); elected by an electoral college through proportional representation by single transferable vote (Article 55).

• Article 52 — There shall be a President of India; Article 61 — impeachment for violation of the Constitution.

question: The split in Indian National Congress occured in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1907.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The famous Surat Split of the Indian National Congress took place in 1907 at the Surat session (Gujarat), presided over by Rash Behari Ghosh. (सूरत विभाजन)

• The Congress split into the Moderates (Garam Dal's rivals — Naram Dal) led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Dadabhai Naoroji and Pherozeshah Mehta, and the Extremists (Garam Dal) led by Lal–Bal–Pal (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal).

• The chief causes were disagreement over the presidentship and over extending the Swadeshi and Boycott movement beyond Bengal.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The two groups reunited at the Lucknow session in 1916, where the Lucknow Pact between the Congress and the Muslim League was also signed.

• 1905 — the Partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon, which triggered the Swadeshi Movement.

• 1906 — the Calcutta session under Dadabhai Naoroji adopted 'Swaraj' as the goal; the Muslim League was founded at Dhaka the same year.

NOTE

• The INC was founded on 28 December 1885 by A. O. Hume; its first president was W. C. Bonnerjee and the first session was held in Bombay.

• Annie Besant (1917) was the first woman president of the INC; Sarojini Naidu (1925) was the first Indian woman president.

question: Which among the following is an example of Angiosperm in Plant Kingdom?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tomato.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Angiosperms are flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed inside a fruit (ovary); 'angio' = covered, 'sperma' = seed. (आवृतबीजी)

• Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is an angiosperm — a dicot of the family Solanaceae, which also includes potato, brinjal and chilli.

• Angiosperms are divided into monocotyledons (one cotyledon, e.g., wheat, rice, maize) and dicotyledons (two cotyledons, e.g., tomato, pea, mango).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Pinus is a gymnosperm — a naked-seeded plant with cones and no fruit.

• Chara is a green alga belonging to the division Thallophyta.

• Funaria (moss) is a bryophyte, called the 'amphibian of the plant kingdom'.

NOTE

• Plant kingdom divisions: Thallophyta → Bryophyta → Pteridophyta → Gymnosperms → Angiosperms.

• Pteridophytes (e.g., ferns, Marsilea) are the first plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem); bryophytes lack true roots.

• Double fertilisation and the presence of true flowers and fruits are unique to angiosperms.

question: When volcano erupts on Earth, the erupted material is typically a liquid rock known as ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lava.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Magma is molten rock beneath the Earth's surface; once it erupts and flows out on the surface it is called lava. (लावा)

• On cooling and solidifying, lava forms extrusive igneous rocks such as basalt; the Deccan Traps of India were formed by such lava flows.

• Volcanoes are classified as active (e.g., Barren Island, India's only active volcano, in the Andaman Sea), dormant and extinct.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Plasma is the fourth state of matter — an ionised gas found in stars, lightning and fluorescent lamps.

• Hailstone is a lump of ice formed in cumulonimbus clouds during a thunderstorm.

• Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature, and also the smallest planet and the one closest to the Sun.

NOTE

• The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean has about two-thirds of the world's active volcanoes.

• Mauna Loa (Hawaii) is the world's largest active volcano; Ojos del Salado (Chile–Argentina) is the highest volcano.

• Magma that cools inside the crust forms intrusive igneous rocks like granite.

question: Four ashrams were recognised by Brahmins around the time when Jainism and Buddhism were becoming popular. Which of the following was NOT a recognised ashrama?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Parmarth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The four ashramas of Vedic/Brahmanical society were Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sanyasa. 'Parmarth' was not one of them. (चार आश्रम)

• Brahmacharya — the student stage, devoted to study of the Vedas and celibacy; Grihastha — the householder stage of marriage, family and worldly duties.

• Vanaprastha — retirement to the forest for meditation; Sanyasa — complete renunciation of worldly life in the pursuit of moksha.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The ashrama system belongs to the Later Vedic period and was formalised in the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras, around the time Jainism and Buddhism arose (6th century BCE).

• The four Purusharthas (aims of life) are Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.

• The four varnas were Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra.

NOTE

• Jainism — 24 Tirthankaras; Rishabhanatha the first and Mahavira the 24th; the Triratna are Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.

• Buddhism — founded by Gautama Buddha; Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path; the first Buddhist Council was held at Rajgriha under Ajatashatru.

question: The Centre scrapped Article 370 of the Constitution in 2019. This article granted special status to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jammu and Kashmir.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 370 was a temporary provision in Part XXI of the Constitution that granted special autonomous status to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. (अनुच्छेद 370)

• On 5 August 2019 the Government of India abrogated the special status by a Presidential Order, and Parliament passed the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.

• With effect from 31 October 2019 the State was reorganised into two Union Territories — Jammu and Kashmir (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without a legislature).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Article 35A, introduced by a 1954 Presidential Order, allowed the J&K legislature to define 'permanent residents' and their special rights; it too ceased to operate in 2019.

• The Union Home Minister at the time was Amit Shah, and the President was Ram Nath Kovind.

• In December 2023 the Supreme Court upheld the abrogation of Article 370.

NOTE

• Article 371 and 371A–371J provide special provisions for states such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa and Karnataka.

• After reorganisation, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories; Ladakh's capitals are Leh and Kargil.

question: Who among the following was awarded with 'Padma Vibhushan' in the year 1986 and choreographed famous song 'Kahe Chhed Mohe' from the movie Devdas and 'Mohe Rang Do Laal' from Bajirao Mastani?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Birju Maharaj.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pandit Birju Maharaj (1938–2022) was the doyen of the Kathak dance form, belonging to the Lucknow 'Kalka-Bindadin' gharana. (कथक नृत्य)

• He was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1986, India's second-highest civilian honour.

• He choreographed 'Kahe Chhed Mohe' (Devdas, 2002) and 'Mohe Rang Do Laal' (Bajirao Mastani, 2015), for which he won the National Film Award for Best Choreography (2016); he also choreographed for 'Vishwaroopam' and 'Dedh Ishqiya'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Uday Shankar — pioneer of modern Indian dance, who blended Indian classical dance with European stagecraft; his film 'Kalpana' (1948) is a classic.

• Bipin Singh — the leading guru of Manipuri dance.

• Kelucharan Mohapatra — the legendary guru of Odissi, and the first performing artist to receive the Padma Vibhushan (2000).

NOTE

• Eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Order of civilian awards: Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri.

question: India has celebrated 76th Independence day in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2022.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India became independent on 15 August 1947; the first Independence Day was celebrated in 1947, so 15 August 2022 marked the 76th Independence Day (and the completion of 75 years of freedom). (स्वतंत्रता दिवस)

• The year 2022 was celebrated as 'Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav', along with the 'Har Ghar Tiranga' campaign.

• The Prime Minister hoists the national flag at the Red Fort, Delhi and addresses the nation; on Republic Day (26 January) the President unfurls the flag at Kartavya Path.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• India's independence was granted under the Indian Independence Act, 1947, based on the Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947).

• Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of British India and the first Governor-General of independent India; C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General.

• Jawaharlal Nehru delivered the 'Tryst with Destiny' speech on the midnight of 14–15 August 1947.

NOTE

• The National Flag was adopted on 22 July 1947; it was designed on the basis of the flag by Pingali Venkayya.

• The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, and India was declared a sovereign, democratic republic.

question: Which of the following is a traditional folk dance of Rajasthan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ghoomar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ghoomar is a famous traditional folk dance of Rajasthan, performed by women in flowing ghagharas who move in circles — the name comes from 'ghoomna', to twirl. (घूमर)

• It is associated with the Bhil community and was adopted by the Rajput royal families; it is performed on festivals such as Teej, Gangaur and Holi and at weddings.

• Other folk dances of Rajasthan include Kalbeliya (a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2010), Kathputli, Chari, Bhavai, Terah Taali and Gair.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Giddha and Bhangra are folk dances of Punjab — Giddha is performed by women and Bhangra chiefly by men during Baisakhi.

• Bihu is the folk dance of Assam, performed during the Bihu festival in April (Rongali Bihu).

NOTE

• Folk dance pairs: Garba/Dandiya — Gujarat; Lavani — Maharashtra; Chhau — Jharkhand/Odisha/West Bengal; Yakshagana — Karnataka; Rouf — Jammu & Kashmir; Cheraw (bamboo dance) — Mizoram.

• Rajasthan's capital is Jaipur; it is India's largest state by area.

question: Ustad Zakir Hussain is one of the greatest exponents of _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tabla.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ustad Zakir Hussain (1951–2024) was the world's foremost tabla maestro, a percussion instrument of Hindustani classical music. (तबला — अवनद्ध वाद्य)

• He was the son and disciple of the legendary tabla player Ustad Alla Rakha.

• He received the Padma Shri (1988), Padma Bhushan (2002) and Padma Vibhushan (2023), along with multiple Grammy Awards; he co-founded the fusion group Shakti with John McLaughlin.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Sitar — Pandit Ravi Shankar, Ustad Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee, Anoushka Shankar.

• Violin — L. Subramaniam, M. S. Gopalakrishnan, N. Rajam, Lalgudi Jayaraman.

• Shehnai — Ustad Bismillah Khan, who received the Bharat Ratna in 2001.

NOTE

• Instrument categories: Tata vadya (string — sitar, sarod, veena), Sushira vadya (wind — flute, shehnai), Avanaddha vadya (percussion with membrane — tabla, mridangam, pakhawaj), Ghana vadya (solid — manjira, jaltarang).

• Other pairs: Sarod — Amjad Ali Khan; Flute — Hariprasad Chaurasia; Santoor — Shivkumar Sharma; Mohan Veena — Vishwa Mohan Bhatt; Mridangam — Palghat Mani Iyer.

question: According to 2011 Census, what is the population density of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 382 persons per square kilometre.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per the Census of India 2011, the population density of India is 382 persons per square kilometre (up from 325 in 2001). (जनसंख्या घनत्व)

• India's total population in 2011 was 121.09 crore (1.21 billion), with a decadal growth rate of 17.7% and a sex ratio of 943 females per 1000 males.

• The literacy rate in 2011 was 74.04% (male 82.14%, female 65.46%).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Among Union Territories, Delhi has the highest density (11,320) and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands the lowest.

• Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state and Sikkim the least populous.

NOTE

• The 2011 Census was the 15th National Census and the 7th after Independence; its motto was 'Our Census, Our Future'.

question: The Third Battle of Panipat took place in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1761.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on 14 January 1761 between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) of Afghanistan. (पानीपत का तृतीय युद्ध)

• The Marathas, led by Sadashiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao (with Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao as head of state), suffered a crushing defeat, which shattered Maratha ambitions of ruling all of India.

• Abdali was supported by Najib-ud-Daula of Rohilkhand and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• First Battle of Panipat (1526) — Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire; Babur used tulughma tactics and field artillery.

• Second Battle of Panipat (1556) — Akbar's forces under Bairam Khan defeated Hemu (Hemchandra Vikramaditya).

• 1757 — the Battle of Plassey, where Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah; 1764 — the Battle of Buxar, followed by the Treaty of Allahabad (1765).

NOTE

• Panipat is in present-day Haryana.

• Other key battles: Battle of Haldighati (1576) — Akbar vs Maharana Pratap; Battle of Talikota (1565) — end of Vijayanagara's dominance; Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — British defeated the French.

question: Olympic Winter Games Beijing 2022 took place in ______.
solution_text:

• The XXIV Olympic Winter Games were held in Beijing, China from 4 to 20 February 2022. (शीतकालीन ओलंपिक)

• The mascot was Bing Dwen Dwen (a panda) and the motto was 'Together for a Shared Future'; Norway topped the medal tally.

Additional Information

• India was represented by a single athlete, skier Arif Khan, in the alpine skiing events.

• The first Winter Olympics were held at Chamonix, France in 1924.

• The 2026 Winter Olympics are scheduled at Milan–Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy, and the 2030 Games in the French Alps.

NOTE

• The International Olympic Committee (IOC) was founded in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin; its headquarters is at Lausanne, Switzerland.

• The Olympic motto is 'Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter' (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together); the Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics were held in 2021 and Paris hosted the 2024 Summer Olympics.

question: As per census 2011, what is the position of Maharashtra with respect to the total population in India?
